nameStory: This crab gets its "iridescent" name from the beautiful rainbow-like shimmer that plays across its shell, especially when wet or under bright light. The shimmering effect comes from microscopic structures in the shell that bend light like tiny prisms. "Swimming" refers to its flattened paddle-like rear legs that make it an excellent swimmer, unlike many crabs that mostly crawl along the bottom.
description: The Iridescent Swimming Crab is a small to medium-sized marine crab with a distinctive shimmery shell that catches the light beautifully. Adults typically reach about 2-3 inches across the shell, making them smaller than the familiar blue crabs many people know. Their bodies are somewhat flattened and streamlined for swimming, with powerful claws and distinctive paddle-shaped back legs. The overall color is usually brownish or olive-green with that characteristic iridescent sheen that gives them their name.

idTips.label: Iridescent Shell
idTips.description: The shell displays a rainbow-like shimmer, especially when wet - hold it up to sunlight and watch colors dance across the surface like oil on water

idTips.label: Paddle-shaped Back Legs
idTips.description: The last pair of legs are flattened into oval paddles that feel stiff and slightly flexible, perfect for swimming through water

idTips.label: Shell Texture
idTips.description: The shell feels smooth with small granular bumps, and has a series of small teeth along the front edge that you can feel with your fingertip

idTips.label: Size and Build
idTips.description: About 2-3 inches wide with a streamlined, somewhat flattened body that feels surprisingly light for a crab

idTips.label: Claw Shape
idTips.description: Claws are moderately sized with pointed tips and feel sturdy but not massively heavy like a lobster's claws

habitat: Found in shallow coastal waters along New England's sandy and muddy bottoms, typically in depths of 10-60 feet. They prefer areas with good water circulation near harbors, bays, and estuaries where they can both swim freely and burrow into soft sediments. Often found around eelgrass beds and areas where fresh and salt water mix.

seasonality.spring: Begin moving into shallower waters as temperatures warm. This is when you're most likely to spot them swimming near the surface or washed up after storms.
seasonality.summer: Most active and commonly encountered during warm months. Peak time for observing their swimming behavior and iridescent shell colors.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to move to deeper waters. Late fall storms may wash specimens onto beaches.
seasonality.winter: Move to deeper, warmer waters and become much less active. Rarely encountered during cold months except as empty shells on beaches.

funFact: These crabs can actually swim backwards faster than they can swim forwards, using their paddle legs like tiny outboard motors to rocket away from danger tail-first!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with blue crabs, but blue crabs are much larger (up to 9 inches wide) and lack the distinctive iridescent shimmer. Remember: if it sparkles like a disco ball in the sun, it's probably an Iridescent Swimming Crab!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "swimming" crabs, they actually spend most of their time on the bottom and only swim when threatened or hunting. The swimming crab family includes many species that aren't particularly good swimmers, so don't expect to see them doing laps!
compareHints: The closely related Blotched Swimming Crab lacks the distinctive iridescent quality and instead has more obvious dark blotches or spots on its shell. Blotched Swimming Crabs also tend to be slightly larger and have a more mottled, less uniform coloration. If you see rainbow shimmer, you've got the Iridescent species; if you see distinct dark patches, it's likely the Blotched variety.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The Blotched Swimming Crab differs from its close relative, the Iridescent Swimming Crab, primarily in color pattern - while both have the characteristic swimming paddles, the Iridescent species has a more uniform coloration with rainbow-like sheens rather than distinct dark blotches.
